page.title: The Problem Queue — propose a world problem | BGET
page.description: Propose any world problem — climate, water, energy, education, civic tech. BGET reads every submission personally, publishes only what we might act on, and every problem gets an answer.
page.ogDescription: A short, honest, public queue of world problems this community might work on next — proposed by anyone, read by a person, every one answered.

hero.h1: What world problem should we work on next?
hero.lead: BGET is a community of builders, scientists, makers and thinkers. Our door is simple: propose any problem you believe the world hasn't solved — from clean water to civic tech — and a person here will read it. Not everything gets published. Everything gets read. The strongest problems enter a public queue where you can watch their status and join the discussion.
hero.trust: No automation. No pay-to-play. Every submission is read by a person — and if we act on yours, you'll be told.

founderNote.quote: I read every problem that reaches the queue myself, usually within two weeks. Every submission gets an answer — shipped, routed, closed with a reason, or published — and silence is a broken promise here.

steps.title: Propose
steps.text: Five minutes, no account needed. Name the problem, say who it affects, and describe what “solved” would actually look like. One link as evidence is plenty.

steps.title: We read it
steps.text: A person on the BGET team reads every submission — usually within two weeks. You always receive an acknowledgment.

steps.title: It joins the queue
steps.text: If your problem is a strong candidate, it appears on our public queue as Under review — with your name if you want it, or anonymously. You're welcome to discuss it.

steps.title: It moves, or it closes
steps.text: If we pursue it, the status advances through Being scoped and In the labs, or we route it to a nonprofit partner already doing this work. Every problem ends with an answer: shipped, routed, or closed — with the reason.

earnsTitle: What earns a place in the queue
earns: It's real and specific. It happens to real people today — not a far-off hypothetical. You can say who it affects and roughly how many.
You can name “solved.” A clear finish line beats grand intent. “Every household outside the municipal line has tested-safe water within 18 months” beats “fix the water crisis.”

It's under-worked. Already-solved problems are still welcome — we'll route you to the people doing it well. The problems we love most are the ones where a few more good people can still move the needle.
It fits what we can actually do. BGET is builders, scientists, makers and thinkers, with nonprofit partners. If there's a path where character and craft can help, it belongs here.
doesnt: Already-solved problems. If an organization is already doing exactly this well, the queue is the wrong home — we'll route you to them instead.
Promotions. “We built X, please fund us” is a pitch. The queue is for problems, not announcements.
Blame. A good problem names a system, not a person. We won't publish anything that targets or shames individuals.
Trivia. “Water is wet” isn't a problem yet. Give it a shape — who, where, what “solved” — and we'll read it.
privacyNote: Public display is a choice, never a default. Most submissions appear nowhere except a private reading pile — but “not published” never means “not read.” If you want your problem in the queue, it's published anonymized by default: no email, no full name, no handle. You choose whether your first name, city and role are shown. We never sell, share or scrape your details, and we never publish anything you asked us to keep private.
queueSub: A deliberately small, curated list. Status changes are made by a person, one row at a time — and every closed problem shows its reason.

statuses.label: Under review
statuses.blurb: Received, read, and being considered. Every published problem starts here.

statuses.label: Being scoped
statuses.blurb: Worth pursuing. A small team is defining the first move: evidence, who's already working on it, and what one good push could be.

statuses.label: In the labs
statuses.blurb: Active work — building, researching, prototyping, or convening with partners.

statuses.label: Shipped
statuses.blurb: It moved. A tool, a report, a prototype, or a handoff to a partner — with a note on what changed.

statuses.label: Closed
statuses.blurb: We won't pursue it, and you get an honest reason: duplicate, out of scope, already solved elsewhere, or no path where we can help.

problems.title: Safe drinking water for households outside the municipal grid
problems.summary: In many fast-growing cities, the formal water network stops at the municipal line. Households beyond it buy water by the jerrycan at 5–10× the network price — often from trucks or kiosks nobody tests. It's a distribution and verification problem as much as a supply problem.

problems.title: Wasted energy in dense cities — heat, idle buildings and the midnight grid
problems.summary: Cities waste a shockingly large share of the energy they buy: buildings cooled and lit while empty, heat dumped from data centres and industry, and grid load that peaks while renewable supply idles. The pieces exist — measurement, controls, pricing — but almost nobody connects them across buildings the way we connect phones.
problems.location: Dense cities worldwide — start: one district

problems.title: Primary care that reaches people who can't reach a clinic
problems.summary: Millions live within a few hours' walk of a clinic but years away from a doctor who can act — diagnosis, prescriptions, and follow-up all break down at the last mile. The gap is less exotic medicine than boring logistics: training, protocols, supplies, and a feedback loop that keeps care honest.

submitTitle: Put a problem in the queue
submitSub: Five minutes, no account, read by a person. Private by default; public only if you choose.
submitNote: You'll get an email the moment we read it.

partnerNote.heading: The honesty clause — partners, credit, and the nonprofit route
paragraphs: BGET is a community, not a nonprofit — and there is no invented one here. Labs output is public-good by default: open tools, free education, research, and handoffs to organizations already doing the work. When a submission is really a nonprofit's job, we say so, route you there, and name the organization publicly.

When BGET Labs produces something a charity could sustain, the founding team will help form — or find — a real legal home for it before any money moves. Impact determines the path: some projects stay open source, some become companies, some become nonprofits, some simply help one community.
This queue and the community share one rule: character before capability. It is better to name a small problem accurately than a big one vaguely.

faq.a: Only if you choose it. Public display is opt-in, anonymized by default. Either way your submission is read, and you always receive an answer.

faq.q: What if you're already working on mine?
faq.a: We'll tell you where it sits in the queue and how it's progressing — or route you to an organization already doing the work, named publicly.
Usually within two weeks. The acknowledgment arrives the moment your submission lands; the answer arrives whether the problem is published or not.

faq.q: Do I get credit if you act on my problem?
faq.a: Yes. Your name appears on the queue card and in the shipped note — unless you ask otherwise. The problem keeps your framing; we never take credit for your idea.

faq.q: Can I submit on behalf of a community?
faq.a: Strongly encouraged. Say who you represent and roughly how many people it affects — community-anchored problems are exactly the ones a small team can actually move.

faq.q: What happens right after I submit?
faq.a: You get an automatic receipt with a reference number, then a personal read, then a status that moves or closes with a reason. Every problem in this queue ends with an answer.

cta.label: The first problem almost never comes from a committee.
